GOAL.label: Working title
GOAL.value: Sleep, Stress and Study Time: What Links Sleep to Exam Scores in Undergraduates

GOAL.label: Problem
GOAL.value: Students who sleep more tend to score higher, but the same students also study more and report less stress. It is unclear how much of the link is sleep itself.

GOAL.label: Objective
GOAL.value: Estimate the exam-score gap between students sleeping 7 h or more and those sleeping less, and how much of it runs through stress and study time.

GOAL.label: Scope
GOAL.value: Everything that could explain the link, including caffeine, exam timing and diet.

GOAL.label: Success criteria
GOAL.value: Each sub-question gets one number with a 95% range, and the write-up says plainly what that number does and doesn't show.

COMPUTE.label: CPU sandbox · 4 cores · 16 GB · no GPU
COMPUTE.detail: Regression, mediation and bootstraps finish in minutes. Nothing in this question needs a GPU.

ESTIMATES.text: Sleep accounts for roughly a quarter of the variation in grades.
Short sleepers score about 10 points lower.

ESTIMATE_CHECKS.note: Sleep measures explained nearly 25% of the variance in grades.
No shortlisted paper reports a gap this size on a 0–100 exam. Dropped; the run will measure it instead.

SCOPE_ADJUSTED.to: Sleep, stress, study time and screen time in undergraduates. Caffeine, diet and exam timing become stated limits.
SCOPE_ADJUSTED.reason: Each of those is a literature of its own and would triple the search without answering your topic.

CARDS.problem: Does everyday sleep predict grades in a real course?
CARDS.method: Fitness trackers over a semester, linked to exam results.
CARDS.metrics: Sleep duration, quality, consistency; exam scores.
CARDS.findings: Sleep measures explained nearly 25% of the variance in grades.
CARDS.limitations: Study time wasn't measured, so sleep can't be told apart from study habits.

CARDS.problem: Is poor sleep a hidden cause of low grades?
CARDS.method: Survey of sleep quality against GPA.
CARDS.findings: Poorer sleep quality went with lower GPA.
CARDS.limitations: Study time and workload weren't controlled.

CARDS.problem: Why are college students so sleepy, and what does it cost?
CARDS.findings: Stress, screens and irregular schedules drive short sleep; sleepiness tracks lower grades.
CARDS.limitations: Causes are listed one by one, never tested together with study time.

CARDS.problem: How does sleep loss affect learning and school results?
CARDS.method: Review of experimental and survey studies.
CARDS.findings: Sleep loss weakens learning capacity and academic results.
CARDS.limitations: Few adult students; stress as the link is barely tested in them.

CARDS.problem: How do college students sleep, and what disturbs it?
CARDS.findings: Stress was the strongest predictor of disturbed sleep.

CARDS.problem: How strong is the sleep–school performance link overall?
CARDS.data: Pooled studies of children and adolescents.
CARDS.findings: Sleepiness and poor sleep quality link more strongly to performance than sleep length.
CARDS.limitations: Children and adolescents only; adults and stress as the link are untested.

CARDS.problem: Do teen sleep schedules relate to daytime functioning?
CARDS.findings: Students with lower grades slept less and went to bed later.

CARDS.problem: Does social media use go with poor sleep in young adults?
CARDS.findings: More social media use went with more sleep disturbance.
CARDS.limitations: Screens were tied to sleep, not to grades.

CARDS.problem: How much does sleep deprivation hurt performance?
CARDS.findings: Sleep deprivation clearly lowers performance, mood most of all.

CARDS.problem: What does sleep do for memory?
CARDS.findings: Sleep actively consolidates newly learned memories.
CARDS.limitations: Lab memory tasks, not real exams.

CARDS.problem: How does sleep shape memory and brain plasticity?
CARDS.findings: Different sleep stages support different kinds of learning.

CARDS.problem: How do you test whether a link runs through something else?
CARDS.findings: Sets out the steps for testing mediation.
CARDS.limitations: Assumes the order of cause is known.

TENSION.text: C1 reads sleep as the cause of better grades. C3 shows stress and workload shape sleep itself, so part of the C1 link may belong to them.

OVERVIEW: Most of the evidence links more and better sleep to better grades, but in school-age samples or without study time measured. A smaller line explains why sleep should help learning, and another shows stress and screens shaping sleep itself. No paper here puts sleep, stress and study time in one model of undergraduates.

GAPS.text: Few papers separate study time from sleep.
Stress as the link is mostly tested in younger students.
Screens are tied to sleep, rarely to grades directly.

RANKING.text: Hold study time fixed while testing sleep. Answers SQ1 and SQ3 at once.
Test stress as the path in undergraduates, where it is barely studied. Answers SQ2.
Tie screens to grades directly. Only one paper to build on, so it comes last.

turns.text: C1 is consistent: more sleep, better grades. First claim: students sleeping 7 h or more score higher, with study, stress and screens held equal.
Testable with a standard student survey: sleep hours, exam score and the three controls. One comparison gives one adjusted difference.
Strong students may simply sleep more. Make the test strict: if the range touches zero, H1 fails.
G2 says stress as the link is untested in adults. Second claim: stress carries part of the sleep effect.
Stress and sleep are usually asked at the same time. The arrow could point the other way.
Then H2 only claims an indirect path exists. If its range includes zero it fails, and the paper says the order is unknown.
G3: screens are tied to sleep, rarely to grades. Third claim: more screen time lowers scores on its own.
One more from G2. If adults are understudied, test whether the effect is stronger after 25.
Few undergraduates are over 25. Expect a very wide range.
Two from Curcio 2006: caffeine could change the sleep effect, and so could exam timing.
Neither is measured in a typical student survey. Both go aside.
Agreed. They go in the paper as limits instead.

H1.statement: Students who sleep 7 h or more score higher.
H1.novelty: Prior work rarely holds study time, stress and screens equal while testing a 7-hour cut-off in one faculty.
H1.rationale: Sleep consolidates what was learned that day, and lost sleep slows performance on tests.

falsify.text: Wrong if the 95% range of the adjusted difference touches or falls below 0 points.

H2.statement: Stress carries part of the sleep effect.
H2.novelty: Stress as the link is mostly tested in school-age adolescents, not in undergraduates.
H2.rationale: Short sleep raises next-day stress, and stress lowers exam performance.

falsify.text: Wrong if the 95% range of the indirect effect includes 0.

H3.statement: More screen time lowers exam scores.
H3.novelty: Screens are tied to poor sleep, but rarely tested against grades directly.
H3.rationale: Screen time takes hours from study and sleep alike.

falsify.text: Wrong if the 95% range of the slope includes 0 or sits above it.

H4.rationale: Older students often work and sleep less regularly, so sleep may matter more.

falsify.text: Wrong if the 95% range of the difference in effects includes 0.
